title: AI designs viruses that can infect bacteria, but only 5% of the time
dek: For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at only about 5%, far from the all-powerful tool the media describes.
why: This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosafety rhetoric, while demonstrating how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.
who: Tech journalists who are half-skeptical of "AI-generated virus" coverage and investors at the AI-biology intersection, plus evidence-based medicine practitioners who need to evaluate observational vaccine studies.
skip: Readers uninterested in vaccine confounding methods can jump straight to the AI phage segment at 38 minutes.

points.h: A vaccine switch as a natural control
points.body: The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to pay more attention to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: those vaccinated before the policy switch got the old vaccine, those after got the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — socioeconomic status, smoking, diet and other unmeasured factors could still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment.

points.h: Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
points.body: How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? Measure it with the E-value. This vaccine study's E-value is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a not-very-strong confounder associated with both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcome" could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 for a conclusion to count as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves admit that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation cannot be treated as evidence.

points.h: AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
points.body: The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence data, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch and had it proven functional. If the media summarises this as "AI directly made a virus", it misses a key point: the model has only seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

points.h: The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
points.body: The prompt given to the model needed only the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome for the accuracy of the output to rise markedly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across all the genomes the model generated. It is like a password meaning "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve freely. This also explains why such a short prompt works — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it hits a functional pressure point.

points.h: AI swaps one gene and adds 58 mutations itself
points.body: The design idea behind EVO36 was not to rewrite the whole genome but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans performed the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI's EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated an extra 58 mutations across the genome. These look like compensatory mutations that let the foreign J protein re-adapt to its local environment. Humans might not think to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where generative models exceed the power of single-point editing.

points.h: Mixed phages specifically target resistant bacteria
points.body: Natural PhiX174 runs into a wall against already-resistant bacteria, failing to break through even after five passages; 16 AI-synthesised phages mixed together infected the previously resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with each other and accumulating new mutations during replication, finally breaking the barrier through collective action. The result suggests that phage therapy should bet not on a single strain but on a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages.

points.h: Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
points.body: For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosafety implications. Vincent objects to that wording directly on the show: the authors have already shown with reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what is needed is not an alarm bell but the start of building a safety framework. He also stresses that as long as you have enough sequence, reconstructing a virus is not science fiction — precisely why a framework is needed rather than fearmongering.

points.h: Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
points.body: Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition but simply because they do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of belief" misdirects policy — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but information outreach so they first learn the vaccine exists.
